text:
OMAHA (DTN) -- Biofuel groups are pressing the IRS and Treasury Department to finalize a rule for the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit as USDA's still-unfinished feedstock carbon calculator leaves farmers and ethanol producers without clear guidance heading into another planting season.

Monday marked the close of the comment period for IRS's update of the rule, which includes changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) to eliminate issues around indirect land use change and foreign feedstocks from outside North America, among other issues.

The proposed IRS rule generated 448 public comments on the Regulations.gov website.

The 45Z tax credit was in the Inflation Reduction Act, originally as one of the incentives to help spur production of sustainable aviation fuel. However, the Biden administration did not finalize rulemaking on how the tax credit would work. Congress then updated the tax credit in the OBBBA last summer.

The tax credit for non-aviation fuel is 20 cents a gallon. The tax credit for sustainable aviation fuel is 35 cents a gallon.

At the same time, biofuel producers could see the tax credit increase fivefold if they follow prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. Those issues are among those that should be adjusted in a final rule, the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association stated in its comments.

"Unfortunately, IRFA has received nearly universal reports that the administrative burden and cost to comply with PWA requirements are crippling the benefit of the program," IRFA stated.

Biofuel groups such as the American Coalition for Ethanol (ACE), Growth Energy and the Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) said the 45Z is critical to the ethanol industry, the rural economy and U.S. energy security.

"If effectively implemented, the 45Z tax credit has the potential to stimulate domestic energy production, strengthen U.S. energy security, bolster rural economies, and support increased investment and innovation in the renewable fuels and agriculture sectors," RFA stated.

ACE noted both ethanol producers and farmers have a lot at stake with the rule. "U.S. corn farmers continue to experience painfully high input costs and low market prices," ACE stated. "Most corn farmers are forecast to suffer their fourth consecutive year of net profit losses in 2026."

For all of that to happen, biofuel groups pressed Treasury and the IRS to move quickly to finalize the regulations around 45Z.

One change in the proposed rule praised by biofuel groups is updating the Greenhouse Gases, Regulated Emissions and Energy Use in Technologies (GREET) model to comply with changes made in the OBBBA last year. The law removed indirect land use as part of the calculation for emissions under the GREET model. RFA called for the Department of Energy (DOE) to more quickly release an updated GREET model for the 45Z.

The OBBBA also ensured feedstocks for the 45Z are limited to the U.S., Canada and Mexico, which will effectively shut down high volumes of imported used cooking oil from China and other countries. Those imports had disrupted the use of soybean oil and other domestic feedstocks by renewable diesel producers.

WAITING ON USDA'S FEEDSTOCK CALCULATOR

The proposed rule includes several layers and steps to recognize farm practices, which includes USDA finalizing its "Feedstock Carbon Intensity Calculator." Once USDA finalizes that, then DOE will adopt a 45Z version of the calculator within the GREET model, and then the IRS would publish additional guidance.

The IRS noted USDA's feedstock calculator is "undergoing testing, peer review and public comment," but USDA has not issued a notice on when that will happen.

Growth Energy pressed the IRS to "adopt reasonable interim measures to allow taxpayers to access emissions reductions from farm practices swiftly and without unnecessary administrative delays."

ACE pointed out farm practices represent about half of ethanol's carbon intensity. With that, biofuel facilities "must have the opportunity to monetize low-carbon farming practices such as reduced tillage or precision fertilizer to fully unlock the value of 45Z." ACE added, "If Treasury allows low-carbon farming practices to qualify toward emissions rates it could mean billions of dollars annually for clean fuel producers and farmers, providing a market-based opportunity to dramatically increase rural and farm income."

USDA has published final technical guidance to quantify, report and verify emission reductions from farm practices. Those technical guidelines were released in January 2025 in the final days of the Biden administration.

The focus of USDA's feedstock calculator is to demonstrate carbon sequestration and lower emissions from farm practices that support no-till or reduced tillage, increase cover crops and reduce fertilizer applications.

DTN reached out to USDA asking about when the department would finalize its feedstock calculator model but did not receive an immediate response on Tuesday.

RFA stated the group generally supports "regenerative feedstock cultivation practices," but the group also raised concerns that USDA's final feedstock calculator "could disadvantage clean fuel producers and farmers in certain regions based solely on their location and uncontrollable geographical factors."

Auditing based on USDA's technical guidelines also "may be overly complex and may discourage" farmers and biofuel producers. RFA called for "simplified and straightforward protocols" to certify and audit farm practices.

Along with that, the slow process of finalizing regulations will once again carry into the start of another crop season. RFA noted spring planting is already underway, and farmers have already made cropping decisions for the year. Farmers and biofuel producers "lacked the information, modeling tools and clear protocols" to leverage regenerative feedstocks for the 45Z credit, RFA stated. "Crops being planted now will be used as feedstock for clean fuel production later this year and well into 2027."

Given those factors, RFA and Growth Energy both called for Treasury to consider using "safe harbor" provisions for biofuel producers making efforts to apply the rules and calculation tools.

ACE has been using a USDA Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP) grant to specifically look at regenerative farm practices and how they are undervalued in different locations in existing models, including USDA's feedstock calculator.

ACE noted Treasury doesn't need to "reinvent the wheel" to deal with verification and recordkeeping for farm practices because USDA agencies already have the tools. ACE pointed to USDA rules for conservation compliance to qualify for government payments. ACE stated Treasury should leverage USDA's existing tools when finalizing 45Z rules.

Growth Energy noted there are other farm practices that reliably quantify emission reductions which could be included in the feedstock calculator, citing the IRS and USDA should look at "biostimulants, biofertilizers and biopesticides" that "enhance soil health, improve nutrient uptake, and increase crop yields."

"It is therefore critical that farmers have flexibility to apply those farm practices that work best for their unique operations, leading to greater incentive and participation."

At the same time, the Trump administration has emphasized a broader effort to end what the president frequently calls "Green New Scam ideologies" and projects. President Trump's new 2027 budget plan details ending "Green New Scam" programs 21 times across the federal government, including USDA and the Energy Department.

Groups representing truck stops, convenience stores and other fuel marketers also weighed in on the 45Z rule with multiple criticisms. Current high gas prices at the pump "should serve as the regulatory North Star of biofuel policy." The groups stated the 45Z does not address affordability challenges for consumers or businesses. The groups called on Congress to reinstate the Biodiesel Blenders' Tax Credit to both bolster soybean demand and help stabilize diesel prices.

"The truth is, '45Z' has failed to help American farmers and American consumers of fuel. Treasury can begin to address these failures by finalizing rules that require transparent disclosure of credit values throughout the fuel supply chain, enabling the economic benefit of the '45Z' Credit to flow to consumers at the pump rather than disappearing in the margins of fuel producers," the fuel marketer groups stated in a joint news release.

title: SHEIN Teams Up with DHL to Cut Air Cargo Emissions with Sustainable Fuel
description:
This service allows corporate customers to support the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in air cargo operations.
In 2025, SHEIN signed a memorandum of understanding with Lufthansa Cargo to explore sustainable air freight technologies and fuel use.
Sustainable aviation fuel comes from renewable or low-carbon sources.
Compared with conventional jet fuel, SAF can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 80%.
Limited Supply, High Costs, Big Potential Sustainable aviation fuel holds promise but also faces hurdles.
text:
SHEIN, the global online fashion and lifestyle retailer, has taken a new step in cutting the climate impact of its logistics. The company signed an agreement with DHL Group to use DHL’s GoGreen Plus service. This service allows corporate customers to support the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in air cargo operations.

SAF is blended into regular jet fuel to reduce carbon emissions from flights. This move is part of SHEIN’s broader work to explore low‑carbon solutions for its air transport footprint.

Mustan Lalani, SHEIN’s Head of Sustainability, remarked:

“Working with partners such as DHL allows us to better understand how sustainable aviation fuel solutions may be incorporated into air cargo logistics. Initiatives like this are part of SHEIN’s broader efforts to explore how emerging approaches across the aviation sector may contribute to addressing carbon emissions associated with air transport.”

What Sustainable Aviation Fuel Is: Cutting Emissions at the Source

DHL’s GoGreen Plus service gives customers lifecycle emissions reductions from SAF. It uses recognized accounting and certification methods. This means SHEIN can include a share of SAF‑related emissions reductions in its corporate reporting.

The collaboration follows earlier deals. In 2025, SHEIN signed a memorandum of understanding with Lufthansa Cargo to explore sustainable air freight technologies and fuel use.

Sustainable aviation fuel comes from renewable or low-carbon sources. These include used cooking oil, agricultural waste, and non-fossil carbon materials. Compared with conventional jet fuel, SAF can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 80%. This is because SAF feedstocks carry less net carbon when burned, considering their origin and life cycle.

Air transport remains a significant source of emissions as global trade and e‑commerce grow. SAF is one of the few scalable solutions available today that can work with existing aircraft engines and fuel infrastructure. It reduces emissions at the source rather than offsetting them after the fact.

SAF is still a small part of global aviation fuel. However, demand and investment are rising due to the industry’s push for net-zero goals. The chart below shows how much SAF is necessary to meet the air transport net-zero target.

Growing Market for SAF: A $16 Billion Industry by 2030

The global sustainable aviation fuel market is expanding rapidly. A recent report by Grand View Research estimates the market was worth US$1.04 billion in 2024. It projects that the industry could reach US$15.85 billion by 2030, growing at a 57.5% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2025 to 2030.

This growth is driven by several factors:

Rising corporate and airline decarbonization targets,

Stronger environmental regulations,

Supportive government policy, and

Increasing investment in SAF technologies.

Airlines and logistics providers are under pressure to cut emissions and invest in cleaner fuel alternatives.

Bio-based SAF comes from plants, waste oils, or renewables. It leads the market since it blends easily with jet fuel, needing few changes to aircraft.

Despite strong projected growth, SAF still accounts for less than 1% of global jet fuel use today. Industry groups, like the International Air Transport Association (IATA), estimate that SAF will supply about 0.7% of aviation fuel by 2025. This is due to slow production growth. By 2030, SAF production ranges from 17 to 20 Mt.

Governments in some regions are introducing mandates to increase SAF usage. For example, the UK requires airlines to blend at least 2% SAF starting in 2025, rising to 10% by 2030 and 22% by 2040. These rules aim to spur SAF production and adoption.

SEE MORE: Heathrow Boosts 2026 Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Incentive 2% Above UK Government Mandate

SHEIN’s Sustainability Goals and Progress

SHEIN has publicly committed to reducing its environmental impact and aligning with climate science goals. The company’s science‑based, net‑zero target has been approved by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). Under this plan, SHEIN aims to reach net‑zero greenhouse gas emissions across its value chain by 2050.

The approved targets include reducing Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% by 2030 and reducing Scope 3 emissions by 25% by 2030. SHEIN also plans to source 100% renewable electricity by 2030 as part of its energy transition.

SHEIN developed a decarboniZation roadmap in 2024 with support from external sustainability consultants. This roadmap guides the company’s emissions reduction efforts and is designed to align with the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.

The logistics footprint — especially Scope 3 emissions from transportation and deliveries — is a major contributor to SHEIN’s overall emissions profile. Exploring low‑carbon fuels like SAF is a practical step in addressing these emissions categories.

Pilots, Traceability, and Carbon Accounting

DHL’s GoGreen Plus service lets customers increase the share of SAF blended into the fuel used in its air cargo network. Under the SHEIN agreement, partners like logistics providers, airlines, and certification frameworks team up. They work to allocate emissions reductions clearly for SHEIN’s reports.

SHEIN’s SAF initiatives include pilot programmes with cargo partners. In 2025, SHEIN procured 187.3 tonnes of SAF for use on 14 Atlas Air charter flights. This reduced an estimated 579.1 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent emissions compared with conventional aviation fuel.

The company is also participating in a SAF pilot in China alongside China National Aviation Fuel (CNAF) and the Second Research Institute of Civil Aviation of China. SHEIN plans to procure SAF through Air China Cargo, using traceability systems to document SAF usage and related emissions benefits.

Moreover, SHEIN joined the World Economic Forum’s Green Fuel Forward campaign. This campaign works to speed up SAF adoption in the Asia-Pacific region. It does this by building capacity, raising awareness, and encouraging collaboration.

Limited Supply, High Costs, Big Potential

Sustainable aviation fuel holds promise but also faces hurdles. Current SAF production capacity is limited, and costs remain significantly higher than conventional jet fuel. This makes widespread adoption difficult for many companies and airlines.

Because SAF is still a small part of the global aviation fuel supply, its current emissions impact is modest. SHEIN acknowledges that the emissions reductions from its initial SAF activities are limited relative to its total air transport footprint. But these pilots will help build experience and partnerships for broader future deployment.

Looking ahead, SAF market growth could ramp up as production capacity rises and regulatory and corporate demand increase. With strong annual growth rates, more companies might add SAF to their supply chains. This helps them meet climate goals and satisfy stakeholders.

For SHEIN, expanding SAF use through partnerships like DHL’s GoGreen Plus could help the company gain operational insights, shape emissions accounting frameworks, and position itself as a participant in emerging low‑carbon logistics solutions.

text:
Sustainable fuel technology provider Velocys and Varhad Capital Pvt Ltd., an India-based biofuel and carbon dioxide removal (CDR) project development company, on April 6 announced the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to advance a new generation of biomass-to-sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) projects in India.

The SAF opportunity in India is driven by abundant agricultural residues, rapidly growing aviation demand, and policy focus on domestic production. The challenge lies in delivering SAF at a favorable cost and scale.

Under the MOU, the companies will engineer and design scalable biomass-to-SAF facilities using indigenous agricultural residues as feedstock. The collaboration combines Varhad's existing operational gasification platform, already producing syngas and biochar from agricultural residues, with Velocys' proven Fischer-Tropsch (FT) technology, enabling a direct and efficient pathway from biomass to SAF. The initial projects will establish a scalable hub-and-spoke model for SAF production in India.

The ultimate objective is to produce Make-In-India SAF that can compete with conventional pathways on cost while achieving strong lifecycle carbon performance.

"With an operating gasification platform already in place, we are moving quickly. Working with Velocys allows us to translate that capability into fuel production through a proven technology that is aligned with favorable market economics," said Prasad Dahapute, founder and managing director of Varhad.

"This collaboration is about combining two commercially proven technologies in a market where we can streamline biomass-to-fuels production with a technically robust, commercially competitive offering," said Sachin Joshi, chief commercial officer at Velocys.

text:
Phelan Green, through its clean fuels arm Phelan eFuels, has announced that it will utilize Honeywell’s advanced renewable fuel processing technology for its upcoming electro-sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) production facility in Saldanha Bay, located in the Western Cape region of South Africa. This strategic technology selection marks an important step in advancing large-scale production of low-carbon aviation fuels in the region.

As part of the project, Phelan eFuels will implement Honeywell UOP’s Fischer Tropsch (FT) Unicracking™ process. This innovative technology converts Fischer Tropsch-derived liquids and waxes—produced using captured carbon dioxide (CO2)—into high-quality eSAF that meets stringent aviation fuel standards. The use of CO2 as a feedstock highlights the project’s strong focus on sustainability and carbon reduction, aligning with global efforts to decarbonize the aviation industry.

Paschal Phelan, Chairman of Phelan Green, emphasized the importance of this technology choice, noting that Honeywell’s Fischer Tropsch Unicracking process offers a reliable and commercially viable pathway for producing sustainable aviation fuel at scale. He described the initiative as a significant milestone not only for the company but also for South Africa’s growing eFuels sector. According to him, the project reflects Phelan Green’s commitment to fostering industrial growth, creating employment opportunities, and investing in forward-looking energy solutions that contribute to emissions reduction.

The planned eSAF facility is a central component of the broader Phelan Green Hydrogen Project, which represents a substantial private investment of approximately R47 billion (around US $2.5 billion). This large-scale initiative has been officially recognized by the South African government as a strategic national development project, underscoring its importance to the country’s economic and environmental goals. Once completed, the facility is expected to rank among the world’s first commercial-scale plants dedicated to eSAF production, with an annual output exceeding 140,000 tons. The fuel produced will primarily be exported to markets in the European Union and the United Kingdom, where demand for sustainable aviation fuels is rapidly increasing due to stricter environmental regulations.

Rajesh Gattupalli, President of Honeywell UOP, highlighted the advantages of the company’s technologies, stating that they are engineered to deliver scalable, efficient, and adaptable solutions for low-carbon fuel production. He added that the deployment of the Fischer Tropsch Unicracking process in this project will play a key role in supporting Phelan eFuels’ objective of establishing commercial-scale sustainable aviation fuel production capabilities in South Africa.

Construction of the Saldanha Bay facility is scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. The development phase is expected to generate thousands of jobs locally, spanning construction, engineering, and operational roles. In addition to boosting employment, the project is poised to strengthen South Africa’s position as a competitive global supplier of next-generation aviation fuels, contributing to the broader transition toward cleaner energy systems.

title: European Investment Bank and Eni Secure €500M Deal For Sannazzaro Biorefinery
description:
The European Investment Bank and Eni have formalized a major financing agreement worth €500 million to support the transformation of a traditional refinery into a modern biorefinery in Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi, located in Italy’s Pavia province.
The project centers on upgrading selected units of the Sannazzaro refinery, particularly the Hydrocracker (HDC2) unit, through the implementation of Ecofining™ technology.
Using its proprietary Ecofining™ process, Enilive produces HVO from renewable sources in compliance with European sustainability regulations.
By leveraging existing infrastructure and utilities at the site, the project will integrate renewable fuel production alongside conventional refining operations.
The Sannazzaro conversion aligns with Eni and Enilive’s broader strategy to scale up biofuel production in response to tightening environmental regulations, including targets outlined in the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III).
text:
The European Investment Bank and Eni have formalized a major financing agreement worth €500 million to support the transformation of a traditional refinery into a modern biorefinery in Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi, located in Italy’s Pavia province. The 15-year loan agreement was signed by EIB Vice-President Gelsomina Vigliotti and Eni Chief Executive Officer Claudio Descalzi, highlighting a shared commitment to advancing cleaner energy solutions and accelerating Europe’s transition to sustainable fuels.

The project centers on upgrading selected units of the Sannazzaro refinery, particularly the Hydrocracker (HDC2) unit, through the implementation of Ecofining™ technology. In addition, a new pre-treatment facility will be constructed to process waste-based raw materials such as used cooking oil, animal fats, and residues from the agri-food sector. These materials will serve as the primary feedstock for Enilive, Eni’s subsidiary focused on sustainable mobility solutions, enabling the production of hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a renewable and low-emission biofuel.

Using its proprietary Ecofining™ process, Enilive produces HVO from renewable sources in compliance with European sustainability regulations. This fuel can be used in its pure form in compatible engines and is already distributed across more than 1,600 Enilive service stations throughout Europe. Beginning in 2028, the upgraded Sannazzaro facility is expected to manufacture both HVO diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with an estimated annual output of approximately 550,000 tonnes.

By leveraging existing infrastructure and utilities at the site, the project will integrate renewable fuel production alongside conventional refining operations. This hybrid approach is designed to lower greenhouse gas emissions in transportation while supporting the decarbonisation of hard-to-abate sectors such as aviation, where SAF currently represents the most viable alternative to fossil fuels. Furthermore, the initiative will diversify fuel supply options, strengthen energy resilience across Italy and the European Union, and contribute to the goals of the REPowerEU strategy by increasing domestic biofuel production capacity.

This agreement builds on a similar €500 million financing deal signed in July 2025 for the conversion of Eni’s Livorno refinery. Together, these projects form part of Enilive’s broader strategy to expand biofuel production capacity to 5 million tonnes annually by 2030, including over 2 million tonnes dedicated to SAF. Currently, Enilive operates biorefineries in Venice and Gela, as well as the St. Bernard Renewables facility in the United States. Additional plants are planned or under construction in Livorno, Malaysia, South Korea, and Priolo in Sicily, the latter in collaboration with Q8.

According to Vigliotti, the financing reflects strong institutional backing for projects that combine environmental sustainability with industrial development, particularly in reducing emissions from aviation. Descalzi emphasized that the agreement demonstrates the strength of Eni’s long-term energy transition strategy, which integrates advanced technologies with scalable industrial operations and a growing customer base. He also noted that biofuels are essential for reducing emissions across multiple transport sectors, including road, maritime, rail, and air travel.

Demand for SAF is projected to increase significantly from 2030 onward, largely driven by regulatory frameworks such as the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation. This anticipated growth supports the long-term economic and technical viability of the Sannazzaro project. At the same time, HVO biofuels are expected to play a crucial role in delivering immediate emissions reductions across transport systems.

The Sannazzaro conversion aligns with Eni and Enilive’s broader strategy to scale up biofuel production in response to tightening environmental regulations, including targets outlined in the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III). Globally, biofuels accounted for about 4% of transport energy consumption in 2024, but this share is expected to rise to 9% by 2035 and 12% by 2050, according to projections from the International Energy Agency’s Net Zero scenario.

text:
Over 50 state ag groups and eight national organizations sent a letter to the International Trade Commission on March 31 urging the agency to revoke the countervailing duty orders on imports of phosphate fertilizer from Morrocco.

The letter – signed by the National Corn Growers Association, American Soybean Association, National Association of Wheat Growers, National Cotton Council, National Sorghum Producers, Society of American Florists, USA Rice, US Rice Producers Association – said that continuing the duties will further worsen the dire economic conditions faced by American farmers.

“Maintaining the phosphate fertilizer [countervailing duties] will allow a small set of powerful corporations to continue to limit supply options for farmers,” the letter said. “This has already prevented farmers from accessing the tools that meet their crop production needs and resulted in lower yields and negative economic impacts.”

The duties stem from a decision in 2020 by ITC to impose duties on phosphate fertilizers imported from Morocco and Russia. The decision came after the U.S.-based Mosaic Company petitioned the agency to do so.

Mosaic claimed at the time that unfairly subsidized foreign companies were flooding the U.S. market with fertilizers and selling the products at extremely low prices. The petition was supported by another U.S. company, J.R. Simplot.

The duties are now being examined under a sunset review process that will determine if they should continue.

The duties have had major effects on the phosphate fertilizer market. At least one Moroccan company halted shipments of phosphate fertilizers into the U.S., which led to price hikes and tight supply conditions, saddling farmers with a hardship that has only become more dire in recent weeks with the conflict in the Middle East. Phosphate (DAP) prices peaked in 2022 during the Russia-Ukraine crisis, but have only eased moderately since, with the corn/phosphate price ratio (the amount of bushels needed to buy a ton of fertilizer) reaching record highs in 2025.

The letter said that these fertilizer companies have gained at the expense of America’s farmer.

text:
Industry stakeholders submitted comments this week to the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service regarding proposed rules on the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit.

The proposed regulations, released on February 3, provide guidance on the determination of clean fuel production credits, emissions rates, and certification and registration requirements. The proposal would extend the credit to Dec. 31, 2029, limit feedstocks to those grown or produced in North America, and eliminate the special rate for sustainable aviation fuel, among other stipulations.

Renewable Fuels Association President and CEO Geoff Cooper says the proposal makes “meaningful progress” in developing rules implementing tax credit, but the top priority for Treasury should be releasing an updated 45ZCF-GREET model as soon as possible.

“The technology-neutral structure of 45Z is a crucial feature, allowing clean fuel producers to pursue the most economically efficient and practical pathways for reducing emissions and boosting domestic energy production,” wrote Cooper in RFA’s comments to Treasury. “However, as currently drafted, certain aspects of the proposal introduce inconsistencies and implementation challenges that may limit participation, create unintended market impacts, and reduce the near-term effectiveness of the program.”

In addition to updating 45ZCF-GREET model, RFA says agencies should work with USDA to finalize and integrate workable, equitable, and science-based technical guidelines for regenerative agriculture feedstocks and an updated Feedstock Carbon Intensity Calculator (FD-CIC). Treasury should adopt a more flexible Provisional Emissions Rate process that allows for efficient characterization of new technologies and incremental emissions-reducing improvements at existing clean fuel facilities, as well as clarifying certain rules, such as the interaction of “undenatured fuel ethanol” and “denatured fuel ethanol” for 45Z credit generation, and that only transportation and industrial fuels are eligible for the credit.

In comments from the American Coalition for Ethanol (ACE), CEO Brian Jennings stressed the significant financial pressure facing rural America and that enabling farmers and producers to benefit from low-carbon practices is critical to unlocking the full value of the 45Z credit.

“Since farming practices represent about half of ethanol’s carbon intensity, clean fuel producers must have the opportunity to monetize low-carbon farming practices such as reduced tillage or precision fertilizer use to fully unlock the value of 45Z,” said Jennings. “If Treasury allows low-carbon farming practices to qualify towards emissions rates it could mean billions of dollars annually for clean fuel producers and farmers, providing a market-based opportunity to dramatically increase rural and farm income.”

ACE also noted the importance of keeping 45ZCF-GREET model and FD-CIC updated with the latest science and real-world data supported through activities such as the USDA Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP) activity being led by ACE and specifically designed to address information gaps regarding the low-carbon benefits of farming practices to help improve the accuracy of modeling tools.

“We have strongly recommended updates to FD-CIC values for low-carbon farming practices by incorporating the best available science and results from real-world activities, so we are encouraged Treasury expects to make these updates as part of future iterations of the 45ZCF-GREET.”

In their comments to Treasury, fuel retailer organizations NATSO, NACS and SIGMA, which represent 90 percent of fuel sold at retail, continue to urge Congress to reinstate the Biodiesel Blenders’ Tax Credit to help stabilize fuel supplies and help lower prices for consumers, claiming that the 45Z tax credit is not helpful.

“The real-world implications on American energy supplies and the price that consumers pay at the pump should serve as the regulatory North Star of biofuel policy…“The ‘45Z’ Credit is not alleviating these affordability challenges for American consumers and businesses. It has not helped American consumers by lowering fuel prices and it has not helped American farmers by increasing sales of corn or soybeans used to produce renewable fuels.”

text:
Clean energy startup Ecoil has raised about $2.5 million in a funding round led by Fundalogical Ventures, with participation from Caspian Impact Investment, Momentum Capital, and existing backer The Chennai Angels, The Economic Times reported.

The company said the fresh funds will be used to expand operations, strengthen its technology platform, and increase its presence across key markets in India.

Founded in 2019 by Sushil Vaishnav and Kirti Vaishnav, Ecoil focuses on collecting and managing used cooking oil from restaurants, hotels, and other food businesses. It uses a technology-driven logistics network to track the oil, ensure regulatory compliance, and channel it for biofuel production.

The startup said used cooking oil is a key raw material for biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), but remains widely scattered across small sources such as eateries and food outlets. In the absence of organised collection systems, the oil often re-enters the food chain, is diverted through informal channels, or is disposed of improperly, posing risks to both public health and the environment.

Investors highlighted the importance of solving supply chain challenges in the biofuels sector. Anil Saldanha said Ecoil is addressing a major bottleneck by enabling reliable feedstock aggregation at scale, especially as demand rises due to biodiesel and SAF blending targets.

Ankur Shrivastava added that while the idea of recycling used cooking oil has been widely discussed, building a traceable and dependable supply chain has remained a challenge. He noted that Ecoil’s model demonstrates that this gap can be addressed, unlocking new opportunities in the biofuel value chain.

text:
The town of Hayward doesn’t see $1.5 billion business opportunities coming its way every day, and even fewer that would connect forestry to sustainable energy. But that’s the idea behind a proposed partnership between a German firm and a local timber business to build a plant that would convert woody biomass into sustainable aviation fuel.

“This facility would use 100-year-old technology known as gasification and Fischer–Tropsch,” said Bill Johnson of Johnson Timbers, the local partner on the project. “We actually worked with this technology in the past during both the Bush and Obama administrations and built a pilot plant utilizing similar technologies down in Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina, using biomass from Wisconsin.”

To help land it, the state Legislature passed an incentive package called the Forestry Revitalization Bill, signed into law last week by Gov. Tony Evers. Johnson and state Rep. Chanz Green of Grand View, a co-sponsor of the bill, joined WPR’s Robin Washington on “Morning Edition” to talk about the project.

The following interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Robin Washington: Tell us about your German partner.

Bill Johnson: Synthec Fuels was formed six years ago. They originally started working on hydrogen technology and were going to build a plant in Germany. The war between Russia and Ukraine broke out, and energy prices spiked. So they decided to switch focus and move to sustainable aviation fuel and started looking at the U.S.

We were introduced to them and showed them the benefits of locating here in the Great Lakes states, emphasizing the workforce, our forest industry knowledge, the strong logging and trucking workforce that we have, and the ability of the ports to be able to move product. They really like the idea of the lake states.

RW: You don’t have to sell us on the benefits of our area. Rep. Green, tell us how your bill will help — and couldn’t they do this without government incentives?

Rep. Chanz Green: We’ve been talking about this now for about four years, and it came to fruition this legislative cycle. We had conversations with everybody, not only Republicans, but Democrats.

Investing in northern Wisconsin became everybody’s priority. Out of 133 legislators, I think we had just seven vote against us. Hopefully bringing this plant to northern Wisconsin will provide jobs and create a little boom town in Hayward.

RW: What are the incentives?

CG: It’s $120 million in tax credits. The money will have to be spent; the project will have to break ground. There are a bunch of buyback provisions. The Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation will be overseeing this. They will make sure that it is fiscally feasible. We’re protecting the taxpayer dollars and their investment.

RW: Aside from the economics, the conversion of forest resources into something sustainable reminds me of what Bayfield County is doing to make their county forests eligible to sell carbon credits, for which they just signed a $2.2 million deal with a Spanish firm. On the one hand, yes, you would still be using the timber, but on the other hand, you’re making something sustainable. And again, a European company paying for it.

BJ: I think as you look at the carbon credit markets, carbon credits don’t necessarily mean not cutting down trees; it’s just cutting to a level that preserves the most carbon.

So as we look at this project, we’re looking at mill residuals that we’re going to be buying. We’re looking at limbs and branches and other things that are left on the forest floor. And then we’re really targeting unmarketable or undesirable species, invasive species, killed wood that is standing dead on the stump, things of that nature.

So I think there’s a place for both carbon credits and this plant to operate in unison and create just a healthy, sustainable forest that we’ve come to know here in Wisconsin. And it’s certainly something that our landowners, our logging professionals and our trucking firms desperately need as we continue to see paper mills close in the region.

text:
Kaunas Airport (KUN) has tested a hydrogen powered truck as part of a wider European initiative to accelerate the adoption of sustainable fuels in airport operations.

The trial forms part of an EU funded project focused on integrating hydrogen into ground handling and airside activities. Led by Lithuanian Airports, the programme is also being conducted at airports in Helsinki, Riga and Tallinn, reflecting growing regional collaboration on decarbonisation.

The hydrogen powered vehicle, developed by Hyzon Motors, was tested across apron, runway and taxiway environments. The heavy duty truck completed operational tasks such as surface cleaning and maintenance without producing CO2 emissions, demonstrating its potential for deployment in day to day airport activities.

According to Modestas Alekna, Head of Sustainable Aviation Projects at Lithuanian Airports, ground transport plays a critical role in achieving wider sustainability goals.

“Green hydrogen is considered a fuel of the future,” he said. “Testing hydrogen powered transport provides valuable operational experience and supports our long term strategy for reducing emissions.”

Testing was carried out over several days, with the vehicle covering approximately 100 kilometres while performing routine airside tasks. Operational planning ensured that any potential disruption to airport activities was avoided, with designated testing zones selected across the airfield.

In addition to the Hyzon truck, a Toyota Mirai passenger vehicle was also trialled, highlighting the broader applicability of hydrogen technology across different vehicle types. Hydrogen supply and refuelling infrastructure for the project was provided by the Latvian Hydrogen Association, ensuring the use of fully renewable hydrogen produced through electrolysis using solar and wind energy.

The trials demonstrated reliable performance, with airport specialists reporting positive results across operational and environmental metrics.

Kaunas Airport was selected for the pilot due to its operational flexibility and lower traffic volumes, enabling controlled testing conditions.

The initiative supports Lithuanian Airports’ target to achieve carbon neutrality by 2030 and aligns with wider European Union ambitions to scale hydrogen as a key energy source for transport decarbonisation by 2050.

title: 'Industry-first': GameChange Solar completes tracker testing for earthquake conditions
description:
GameChange Solar has announced the successful completion of its single-axis solar trackers for earthquake conditions claimed to be the first of its kind in the industry.
The siesmic shake table testing programme for its Genius Tracker system was completed at UC Berkeley’s Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research (PEER) Centre, in accordance with IEEE 693 seismic design standards.
It simulated extreme earthquake conditions representative of high-risk regions such as the New Madrid Seismic Zone, with the testing representing one of the most intense credible seismic scenarios for a US solar installation.
A full-scale tracker system with mounted PV modules was subjected to progressively increasing seismic inputs, including broadband excitation and high-performance-level testing up to 2.5g spectral acceleration.
We now have conclusive evidence that a solar tracking system, such as GameChange’s Genius Tracker, can be designed to withstand the forces associated with a meaningful earthquake.”

Scott Van Pelt, Chief Engineer at GameChange Solar said: “As solar expands into seismic-risk regions like California, Chile and the New Madrid Fault Zone, the industry has had negligible real-world data on how modern utility scale trackers and modules perform in an earthquake.

“This test changes that. We now have conclusive evidence that a solar tracking system, such as GameChange’s Genius Tracker, can be designed to withstand the forces associated with a meaningful earthquake.”

Report Description

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Outlook 2025-2034

The global sustainable aviation fuel production market was valued at $7.2 billion in 2025 and is projected to expand at a remarkable compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 35.0% from 2026 to 2034, reaching an estimated $169.4 billion by 2034, driven by tightening carbon regulations, sweeping airline decarbonization pledges, and rapidly maturing production pathways across multiple feedstock categories. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is now widely recognized as the most pragmatic near-term solution for decarbonizing commercial aviation, a sector responsible for approximately 2.5% of global CO2 emissions and nearly 4% of total climate forcing when non-CO2 effects are accounted for. The momentum behind SAF is unprecedented: in 2025 alone, more than 65 airlines had active SAF off-take agreements, and global SAF production capacity surpassed 1.5 million metric tons per year, roughly double the capacity recorded in 2023. Policy frameworks such as the European Union's ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, which mandates SAF blending ratios rising from 2% in 2025 to 70% by 2050, and the United States' Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) blender tax credits of up to $1.75 per gallon, are fundamentally reshaping the economics of SAF production and creating durable, long-term demand signals for producers and investors alike. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has pledged net-zero aviation by 2050, with SAF expected to contribute up to 65% of the required emissions reductions, making the trajectory of this market almost structurally certain. Additional tailwinds include the deployment of novel production technologies such as Power-to-Liquid (PtL) electrofuels, Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) processes, and advanced Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, all of which are expected to diversify feedstock sourcing beyond conventional bio-based streams and dramatically expand the addressable production base through 2034.

Market Size: 2019: USD Billion 0.6, 2021: USD Billion 1.2, 2023: USD Billion 3.8, 2025: USD Billion 7.2, 2026: USD Billion 9.7, 2028: USD Billion 17.7, 2031: USD Billion 52.4, 2034: USD Billion 169.4. CAGR: 35.0%

The competitive dynamics of the sustainable aviation fuel production industry have evolved substantially since 2019, when global SAF volumes were negligible at barely 25,000 metric tons. By 2025, production exceeded 1.5 million metric tons, and the trajectory toward meeting the IATA's target of 450 million metric tons annually by 2050 is gaining credibility as more greenfield and brownfield projects achieve financial close. Critically, production cost curves are bending: the average production cost of HEFA-based SAF has declined by nearly 18% since 2021, while next-generation PtL pathways benefit from falling renewable electricity prices, which dropped by over 35% in major markets between 2020 and 2025. The catalytic hydrothermolysis jet fuel market also represents a complementary production pathway, further expanding the diversity of SAF supply chains. At the same time, feedstock security is emerging as a central strategic consideration: agricultural waste and municipal solid waste (MSW) streams are being rapidly scaled as alternatives to used cooking oil (UCO), which faces growing supply constraints as demand from the road transport biodiesel sector competes for the same resource pool.

From a policy perspective, 2025 and 2026 have seen a wave of national SAF mandates and incentive structures crystallize across both developed and emerging markets. Japan's Green Transformation (GX) program mandated 10% SAF blending at major airports by 2030. Singapore launched its Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint requiring 1% SAF by 2026, rising to 3-5% by 2030. Brazil's RenovaBio program is expanding its biofuel certificates to include aviation, while India's Ministry of Civil Aviation published a SAF roadmap targeting 1% domestic blending by 2027. These converging regulatory signals, combined with the massive capital influx from major oil majors, airlines, and specialist renewable fuel companies, are expected to sustain the 35.0% CAGR well into the forecast period. The aircraft engine market is closely interconnected with SAF development, as engine OEMs including Rolls-Royce, GE Aerospace, and Pratt & Whitney have committed to 100% SAF-compatible engines by 2030, which will remove the remaining technical barriers to higher blend ratios at scale.

This analysis is based on primary and secondary research conducted through Q4 2025, with data verified as of April 2026.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Regional Outlook 2026-2034

North America dominated the global sustainable aviation fuel production market in 2025, accounting for 36.2% of total market revenue, equivalent to approximately $2.6 billion. The region's leadership is rooted in a combination of robust policy support, mature biorefinery infrastructure, and the highest concentration of SAF off-take agreements globally. The United States remains the anchor, with its Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) providing blender tax credits of $1.25-$1.75 per gallon based on lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction scores under the CORSIA and LCFS frameworks. This has catalyzed a surge of SAF investment, with the U.S. Department of Energy's SAF Grand Challenge targeting 3 billion gallons per year of domestic SAF production by 2030 -- a target requiring approximately $50 billion in capital deployment. Canada is also emerging as a significant SAF producer, leveraging its abundant agricultural waste and forestry residue streams; projects such as Enerkem's waste-to-methanol-to-SAF facilities in Alberta are expected to come online between 2026 and 2028. The region benefits from integrated supply chains connecting Midwest agricultural hubs, Gulf Coast biorefineries, and major hub airports in Chicago, Dallas, New York, and Los Angeles, providing logistical efficiency advantages that will be difficult for other regions to replicate at scale within the forecast period. Airlines including United, Delta, and American have signed multi-year SAF supply agreements totaling hundreds of millions of gallons annually, providing the demand certainty needed to attract infrastructure capital. North America is expected to maintain its leading share throughout the 2026-2034 forecast period, though Asia Pacific will close the gap meaningfully.

Europe held the second-largest share of the sustainable aviation fuel production market at 29.4% in 2025, driven by the EU's aggressive ReFuelEU Aviation regulation and the UK's Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate. The EU mandate requires 2% SAF blending in 2025, scaling to 6% by 2030, 20% by 2035, and 70% by 2050, making Europe the most stringently regulated SAF market in the world. This has spurred significant capacity buildout across the Netherlands, Finland, Germany, France, and the UK, where companies such as Neste (Helsinki), TotalEnergies (France), and bp (UK) are either commissioning or expanding SAF-dedicated production lines. The European SAF market is also characterized by a high share of advanced SAF pathways, particularly Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and Power-to-Liquid, which are eligible for higher regulatory credits and benefit from Europe's developed green hydrogen infrastructure. Germany's H2Global initiative is directly funding electrofuel imports and domestic PtL capacity, while France's green kerosene strategy includes state co-investment in SAF production hubs at Normandy and Toulouse. The region is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 33.5% through 2034 as the compliance demand floor rises with each regulatory milestone. Asia Pacific, meanwhile, is the fastest-growing regional market, expected to expand at a CAGR of 38.2% through 2034, underpinned by China's 14th and 15th Five-Year Plans, Japan's GX initiative, India's SAF roadmap, and Singapore's Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint. Asia Pacific accounted for 22.1% of market revenue in 2025, supported by a large and rapidly expanding commercial aviation fleet, domestic UCO supply chains in Southeast Asia, and substantial government-backed investment in next-generation biofuel infrastructure.

Latin America represented 7.2% of the global sustainable aviation fuel production market in 2025, growing at a CAGR of approximately 31.8% through 2034, with Brazil leading the region through its RenovaBio program and its unmatched sugarcane-to-ethanol-to-SAF production pathway. Brazil's EMBRAER and GOL airlines are among the most active SAF buyers in the region, and the country's feedstock abundance -- including sugarcane bagasse, soybean residues, and eucalyptus -- positions it as a potential major SAF exporter by 2030. Argentina, Colombia, and Chile are also investing in feedstock aggregation infrastructure with international support. Middle East & Africa held a 5.1% share in 2025 and is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 29.5% through 2034. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are leading regional SAF ambitions: Abu Dhabi's Masdar and Saudi Aramco have announced SAF projects leveraging municipal waste, captured CO2, and green hydrogen as feedstocks. The Middle East's geography at the intersection of long-haul aviation routes, combined with plentiful solar energy for green hydrogen and electrofuels, positions the region as a longer-term structural SAF production hub. African nations, particularly Kenya, South Africa, and Morocco, are nascent but fast-developing markets, with feedstock potential from jatropha, camelina, and municipal waste streams attracting pilot project investment from international developers.

Regional Market Share: North America: 36.2%, Europe: 29.4%, Asia Pacific: 22.1%, Latin America: 7.2%, Middle East & Africa: 5.1%

Key Growth Drivers of the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Analysis, By Feedstock

The feedstock segment is a critical determinant of both the economics and the environmental performance of sustainable aviation fuel production. Used Cooking Oil (UCO) dominated the feedstock landscape in 2025, commanding the largest revenue share of 38.4%, equivalent to approximately $2.8 billion. UCO's dominance reflects its mature collection infrastructure, relatively low cost compared to virgin vegetable oils, compatibility with HEFA processing technology, and its established certification under CORSIA and the EU's Renewable Energy Directive (RED II). However, UCO supply growth is inherently constrained: global UCO availability is estimated at approximately 6-8 million tonnes per year, and competition for this feedstock from road transport biodiesel producers (particularly HVO producers in Europe) is intensifying, potentially capping UCO's long-term share of SAF production as volumes scale. The UCO supply tension has prompted regulators in the EU to impose import origin verification requirements, particularly targeting UCO imports from China, which have faced fraud allegations, adding supply security concerns on top of availability constraints. Despite these limitations, UCO-based SAF through HEFA pathways will remain the largest single feedstock category through at least 2028-2029 given the maturity and scale of existing processing infrastructure. The commercial aircraft parts market and its suppliers are increasingly specifying SAF compatibility in maintenance and operations documentation, underscoring the downstream integration of SAF across the aviation value chain.

Agricultural Waste is the second-largest feedstock category, holding a 22.7% share in 2025, and is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 37.5% through 2034, outpacing UCO's growth trajectory. Agricultural residues including corn stover, wheat straw, rice husks, sugarcane bagasse, and forestry byproducts represent a theoretically vast feedstock pool: the U.S. Department of Energy estimates that the U.S. alone could sustainably supply over 1 billion dry tonnes of agricultural and forestry biomass annually. The key challenge is logistics -- these feedstocks are geographically dispersed and require significant collection, preprocessing, and transportation infrastructure before they can be economically used in centralized SAF production facilities. Fischer-Tropsch and AtJ pathways are best suited to process agricultural waste streams, and as these technologies achieve commercial scale between 2026 and 2030, agricultural waste's share of total SAF feedstock is expected to grow substantially. Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) held a 16.3% share in 2025 and is growing rapidly, particularly in Europe where tipping fee economics significantly improve the financial case for waste-to-fuel projects. Companies such as Fulcrum BioEnergy and Enerkem have demonstrated commercial MSW-to-SAF conversion, though scaling to large-volume production remains technically challenging due to feedstock composition variability and residue handling requirements.

Algae as a SAF feedstock represented 11.2% of the market in 2025 and is growing at approximately 41.0% CAGR, one of the fastest rates in the feedstock segment, driven by algae's extraordinary lipid productivity per unit land area -- up to 80 times more oil per hectare than conventional oilseed crops -- and its ability to use wastewater and non-arable land, eliminating land-use competition with food crops. While algae-to-SAF remains relatively expensive at the commercial scale due to cultivation, harvesting, and extraction costs, significant advances in photobioreactor efficiency, open-pond optimization, and genetic modification of lipid content are driving down costs. The U.S. DOE's Bioenergy Technologies Office (BETO) has invested over $200 million in algal biofuel R&D since 2019. Captured CO2 feedstock, used primarily in Power-to-Liquid electrofuel pathways, held an 11.4% share in 2025 and is the fastest-growing feedstock sub-category in percentage terms, with a projected CAGR of approximately 52.3% through 2034, as PtL technology approaches cost competitiveness and green hydrogen infrastructure expands. The convergence of direct air capture scale-up and renewable electricity price compression is expected to make CO2-to-SAF pathways economically viable in the $3-$5 per gallon range by 2032-2034.

Market Share by Segment: Used Cooking Oil: 38.4%, Agricultural Waste: 22.7%, Municipal Solid Waste: 16.3%, Captured CO2: 11.4%, Algae: 11.2%

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Analysis, By Production Technology

Production technology is perhaps the most defining characteristic of SAF supply, determining feedstock flexibility, cost profile, scalability, and carbon intensity. HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) is the unambiguous leader in 2025, accounting for approximately 54.7% of total SAF production capacity. HEFA technology leverages the same hydroprocessing infrastructure used in petroleum refining, enabling rapid capacity additions through co-processing at existing refineries without the need for entirely new, purpose-built plants. The technology accepts a range of lipid-based feedstocks including UCO, tallow, camelina oil, and palm fatty acid distillate (PFAD), processing them via hydrogenation and isomerization to produce SAF with a carbon intensity 50-80% lower than conventional jet fuel depending on the feedstock. Neste's three global refineries -- in Porvoo (Finland), Rotterdam (Netherlands), and Singapore -- collectively produced approximately 500,000 tonnes of SAF in 2025 using HEFA technology, representing the largest single-company contribution to global SAF supply. The primary constraint on HEFA growth is feedstock availability for UCO and conventional vegetable oils; however, new agricultural feedstocks and camelina cultivation programs (notably in the U.S. Great Plains) are expanding the feedstock base. HEFA's CAGR through 2034 is expected at approximately 31.2%, below the overall market growth rate, as newer technologies take market share from a larger base. The aviation carbon fiber market offers interesting synergies with SAF, as both represent core pillars of aviation's weight reduction and emissions reduction agenda simultaneously.

Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis held approximately 17.8% of the production technology segment in 2025 and is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 38.5% through 2034, driven by its unique ability to process a diverse range of solid and gaseous feedstocks including agricultural residues, municipal solid waste, and even gasified coal (though the latter is excluded from SAF certification pathways). FT synthesis works by first gasifying the feedstock to produce syngas (CO + H2), then catalytically converting the syngas to hydrocarbon liquids including jet fuel range fractions. The technology's major advantages are feedstock flexibility and the potential for very high lifecycle GHG reductions (up to 94% for waste-based feedstocks), making it particularly valuable for compliance with the EU's e-fuel mandate under ReFuelEU. Commercial-scale FT SAF plants are being developed by companies including Velocys (UK/US), INFINIUM (US), and Red Rock Biofuels (US), with several facilities targeting first production between 2026 and 2029. Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) represented 16.9% of the production technology segment in 2025 and is expected to grow at approximately 40.2% CAGR through 2034. AtJ converts ethanol or isobutanol -- produced from biomass, agricultural residues, or industrial waste gases -- into SAF through a series of chemical conversion steps. LanzaJet's commercial-scale AtJ facility in Georgia, USA, commissioned in 2023, demonstrated the viability of the pathway at industrial scale and has become a reference point for global AtJ project development. The technology benefits from the existing global ethanol production infrastructure, which provides a scalable feedstock supply chain without requiring entirely new biomass processing systems.

Power-to-Liquid (PtL) electrofuels represented 10.6% of the production technology market in 2025 but are growing at the fastest CAGR of any technology segment at approximately 55.0% through 2034, making them the technology most likely to reshape the SAF market's competitive dynamics by the end of the forecast period. PtL involves electrolysis of water using renewable electricity to produce green hydrogen, which is then combined with captured CO2 in a reverse water-gas shift reaction to produce syngas, which is subsequently converted to SAF via FT synthesis or methanol-to-jet pathways. The appeal of PtL lies in its complete independence from biological feedstocks, its scalability with renewable energy deployment, and the potential for very high lifecycle GHG reductions exceeding 90%. The EU specifically targets PtL electrofuels in ReFuelEU, requiring a 0.7% PtL blending mandate in 2030, scaling to 35% by 2050. Commercial PtL projects in development include Ineratec's Frankfurt e-fuel plant (Germany), HIF Global's facilities in Chile and Texas (targeting 80,000 tonnes/year by 2025-2026), and Norsk e-Fuel's Mosjoen facility in Norway. These projects are expected to add meaningful volumes to the global SAF supply by 2027-2030, with PtL's cost trajectory closely tied to the pace of green hydrogen cost reduction and renewable electricity expansion.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Analysis, By End User

Commercial Airlines constitute the dominant end-use segment of the sustainable aviation fuel production market, accounting for approximately 68.3% of total SAF consumption in 2025. The scale of commercial aviation's fuel demand -- estimated at approximately 300 billion liters per year globally -- makes it both the primary driver of SAF demand and the primary challenge for the SAF supply industry, which currently produces only a tiny fraction of this requirement. However, regulatory mandates, CORSIA compliance obligations, corporate sustainability commitments from major corporates using air travel, and the reputational dynamics of aviation sustainability are all driving commercial airline SAF procurement at an accelerating pace. Major airlines are entering into long-term SAF supply agreements with financial structures that include price floors and volume guarantees, providing producers with the revenue visibility needed to justify capacity investment. In 2025, commercial airlines including Lufthansa Group, IAG (British Airways parent), Air France-KLM, and Korean Air all published expanded SAF procurement commitments as part of their EU ETS compliance strategies. The segment is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 34.1% through 2034, closely tracking overall market growth as SAF penetration into airline fuel schedules rises from approximately 0.5% in 2025 toward potential 5-10% blending rates by 2034. The aerospace insulation market and other aviation subsystem markets are collectively advancing the technical sustainability of the aviation sector alongside SAF adoption.

Military Aviation held approximately 12.4% of the end-use segment in 2025 and is a strategically important SAF demand driver that is often underappreciated in commercial market analyses. The U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) is the world's largest single organizational consumer of jet fuel, consuming approximately 2.5 billion gallons per year, and has set a target to source 10% of its aviation fuel needs from SAF by 2028. NATO's Climate Change and Security Action Plan includes commitments by member states to increase SAF adoption in military aviation, and the UK's Royal Air Force conducted the world's first 100% SAF flight with an operational military aircraft (a Voyager tanker) in 2023. Military demand for SAF is particularly valuable for the industry because defense contracts typically provide long-duration, price-stable off-take agreements with sovereign counterparties, further reducing investment risk for SAF producers. The U.S. Air Force and Navy have been particularly active in testing and certifying SAF blends for military-specific aircraft and engine types, with full certification across the DoD fleet expected by 2027. Business & General Aviation held a 10.8% share in 2025 and is one of the fastest-growing end-use segments on a percentage basis, with a CAGR of approximately 37.8% through 2034. Business aviation's high-net-worth customer base is disproportionately exposed to corporate sustainability disclosure requirements and personal ESG scrutiny, creating strong willingness-to-pay for SAF. Cargo Carriers held the remaining 8.5% share in 2025, with DHL, FedEx, and UPS among the most active SAF buyers in the freight sector.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Opportunities and Threats 2025-2034

The sustainable aviation fuel production market presents a series of exceptional strategic opportunities across the value chain through 2034. The most significant opportunity lies in the feedstock diversification imperative: as UCO supply constraints tighten and regulatory bodies increasingly scrutinize the sustainability of lipid-based feedstocks, there is a critical need and significant first-mover advantage for companies that can successfully develop and commercialize agricultural waste and MSW-based SAF production at scale. Companies that can build integrated feedstock aggregation, preprocessing, and logistics infrastructure for lignocellulosic biomass -- often the largest cost component in cellulosic SAF -- will establish significant competitive moats. The emerging Power-to-Liquid opportunity is equally compelling: the convergence of declining green hydrogen costs, expanding renewable electricity generation, and Direct Air Capture scale-up creates an enormous greenfield market for PtL SAF capacity, particularly in regions with abundant renewable energy resources such as the Middle East, Chile, Australia, and Scandinavia. PtL SAF is attractive because it is theoretically unconstrained by feedstock biology, scalable with energy infrastructure, and eligible for the highest regulatory incentive values in the EU and UK. The book-and-claim market mechanism represents an additional commercial opportunity, enabling SAF producers to access premium corporate sustainability buyers globally regardless of geographic colocation, potentially commanding price premiums of 15-30% above spot SAF prices. Finally, the integration of carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) with biogenic CO2 from SAF production (Bio-CCS) creates potential for carbon-negative SAF production, which could command extraordinary premium prices in voluntary carbon markets and from airlines with net-negative emission targets. The aerospace foam market is among the adjacent aviation materials segments that are also benefiting from the broader trend of aviation sustainability investment.

Emerging markets present a particularly compelling opportunity cluster for the sustainable aviation fuel production industry through 2034. Southeast Asia is home to the world's fastest-growing aviation market and some of the most abundant UCO and agricultural waste feedstock streams, yet SAF production infrastructure is nascent. Companies that establish SAF production capacity in countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam -- where palm oil supply chains already exist, regulatory frameworks are developing rapidly, and governments are eager to build new export industries -- could capture significant market share ahead of the expected demand surge from the region's rapidly expanding commercial aviation sector. Africa represents an even earlier-stage but potentially transformative long-term opportunity: with vast land resources suitable for non-food energy crops, enormous solar energy potential for PtL, and nascent but developing aviation growth, Africa could emerge as a meaningful SAF production hub in the 2030s, particularly if international climate finance mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund and Just Transition mechanisms provide early-stage capital. Brazil's sugarcane-to-SAF pathway is one of the world's most cost-competitive SAF production options, and Brazilian SAF exports to Europe and Asia are expected to scale meaningfully through 2030, presenting a significant revenue opportunity for Brazilian biorefineries and agriculture conglomerates with the infrastructure to integrate SAF into their operations. Corporate sustainability officers' increasing adoption of Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) FLAG (Forest, Land, and Agriculture) frameworks is also creating new demand for SAF certificates with robust land-use sustainability accounting, creating an additional quality differentiation opportunity for producers with the highest-integrity feedstock chains.

However, the sustainable aviation fuel production market also faces meaningful threats and challenges that could moderate its growth trajectory relative to optimistic projections. The most significant is the feedstock competition and supply security risk: the market's current dependence on UCO and conventional vegetable oils makes it vulnerable to agricultural commodity price volatility, weather events, geopolitical disruptions in major feedstock-producing regions, and the increasingly intense competition from road transport biofuel mandates (particularly Europe's revised RED III). If UCO prices rise significantly -- as they did during the 2021-2022 energy crisis -- HEFA SAF production costs can spike dramatically, making SAF temporarily uncompetitive even with policy incentives and forcing airlines to either pay premiums that threaten their profitability or fail to meet blending obligations, potentially triggering regulatory penalties. Political risk is another concern: the U.S. IRA's SAF tax credits face ongoing political scrutiny and could be modified or rescinded in future legislative cycles, creating uncertainty for long-duration investment decisions. Permitting, planning, and environmental approval processes for large-scale SAF production facilities have proven significantly slower and more complex than initially anticipated in many jurisdictions, delaying capacity additions and creating supply shortfalls versus regulatory demand timelines. Finally, the technological risk associated with advanced pathways -- particularly PtL and novel biological conversion routes -- means that anticipated cost reductions may take longer than projected to materialize, particularly if green hydrogen scale-up faces setbacks related to electrolyzer supply chains, grid interconnection delays, or financing constraints in key markets.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Market Competitor Outlook 2025-2034

The competitive landscape of the sustainable aviation fuel production market is rapidly evolving from a niche space dominated by specialist biofuel companies into a multi-sector battleground where oil majors, national energy companies, dedicated SAF startups, and vertically integrated agricultural conglomerates are competing for market position. The market remains relatively fragmented in 2025, with no single company commanding more than 15% of global SAF production capacity, though the scale of capital investment underway is expected to produce a more consolidated industry structure by 2030. Three primary competitive archetypes define the current market: integrated oil and gas majors leveraging refinery conversion economics and global distribution networks (Neste, Shell, bp, TotalEnergies); specialist biofuel and renewable energy companies with proprietary technology platforms (Gevo, LanzaTech/LanzaJet, Velocys, Fulcrum BioEnergy); and new entrants from the green hydrogen and PtL space (Ineratec, INFINIUM, HIF Global). The intensity of competition is expected to increase substantially between 2026 and 2030 as regulatory demand mandates create more predictable revenue streams and as the first cohort of large-scale commercial SAF plants achieves operational validation. Key competitive differentiators in this market include feedstock security and cost (first-mover advantages in aggregating waste feedstock streams are particularly valuable), technology cost curves (companies with proprietary catalysts or process innovations that drive lower conversion costs), off-take agreement quality (long-term agreements with investment-grade airline counterparties provide financing advantages), and geographic proximity to regulatory mandates (EU and U.S. SAF incentive regimes offer the most financially attractive producer economics). The aircraft actuator market and other aviation subsystems are tangentially impacted by the SAF transition, as aircraft manufacturers and operators adjust maintenance and operations protocols for higher-blend SAF environments.

Neste (Finland) is the clear global leader in SAF production capacity in 2025, with approximately 500,000 tonnes per year of SAF production across its Porvoo, Rotterdam, and Singapore refineries. Neste's competitive advantage lies in its unmatched scale in HEFA technology, its global feedstock sourcing network spanning over 50 countries, its established relationships with airlines and SAF offtakers, and its continuous capital investment in both capacity expansion and feedstock diversification (including camelina oil and algae). In 2025, Neste announced plans to expand its Rotterdam refinery capacity to increase SAF output by an additional 100,000 tonnes per year by 2027. Neste's strong balance sheet and its position as the only pure-play publicly listed renewable fuel major give it a structural advantage in attracting capital for capacity expansion. Shell is aggressively building its SAF position from a base of petroleum distribution infrastructure, investing heavily in its Rotterdam Energy and Chemicals Park for PtL SAF production and developing SAF blending and distribution capabilities at major airports globally, including Schiphol, Heathrow, and Singapore Changi. Shell's competitive strategy centers on integrating SAF into its existing aviation fuel supply agreements, leveraging its dominant market share in conventional jet fuel distribution to cross-sell SAF as a premium sustainability product with minimal incremental logistics cost.

bp is investing over $1 billion in SAF production capacity at its Castellon refinery in Spain and has established a dedicated SAF business unit, bp Aviation Fuels, which manages SAF supply agreements with over 30 airlines globally. bp's Castellon project is among the largest individual SAF capacity additions planned in the 2025-2027 period, targeting 800,000 tonnes per year of renewable fuel output, a significant portion of which will be allocated to SAF. World Energy operates the world's first commercial SAF production facility at its Los Angeles refinery (commissioned 2016) and has been a consistent supplier to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), the first major U.S. hub to offer a sustained SAF supply. World Energy is expanding its SAF production footprint across the U.S. in partnership with the Air Force and multiple commercial airlines, targeting production capacity growth of approximately 300% by 2028 through refinery expansions and new facility development. Gevo Inc. is advancing its proprietary isobutanol-to-SAF pathway through its Net-Zero 1 project in South Dakota, which targets production of 65 million gallons per year of SAF and other renewable fuels upon full commissioning, expected by 2026-2027. Gevo's technology is distinguished by its potential to produce SAF from corn stover and other agricultural residues with near-zero lifecycle carbon intensity when combined with carbon capture at the production facility, qualifying for the highest IRA tax credit tiers. LanzaTech, operating through its LanzaJet subsidiary, has pioneered the commercial-scale Alcohol-to-Jet pathway with its Freedom Pines facility in Georgia, USA, and is licensing its technology to multiple international developers in Japan, the UK, and China. TotalEnergies is converting its La Mede refinery in France to dedicated SAF production and expects to supply 285,000 tonnes per year of SAF by 2027, targeting European airline customers under ReFuelEU compliance obligations.

The competitive landscape is further shaped by a growing ecosystem of feedstock companies, technology licensors, and infrastructure providers that compete and collaborate across the SAF value chain. Feedstock aggregators and waste management companies including Clean Earth Capital, Circular Fuels, and Rialto Energy are establishing strategic positions in the collection, processing, and supply of MSW and agricultural waste feedstocks to SAF producers, capturing value at the upstream end of the supply chain. Engineering and technology companies including Haldor Topsoe (now Topsoe), Honeywell UOP, and Axens are licensing their SAF process technologies globally, with hundreds of projects at various development stages incorporating their proprietary catalysts and reactor designs. Airlines are also increasingly acting as strategic investors in SAF producers to secure future supply: United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, and Lufthansa have all made direct equity investments in SAF production companies, blurring the traditional boundary between producer and customer. This vertical integration trend is expected to intensify through the forecast period as the most strategically sophisticated airlines seek to insulate themselves from SAF price volatility and supply security risk by internalizing a portion of their SAF supply chain.
